summary: Describes how to carry voicemail messages over Internet mail as part of a unified messaging setup. Internet Voice Messaging is not a successor to VPIM version 2 but an alternative specification for a different application. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This lets a voice message travel like a normal email, so you can listen to it from your inbox. It is a different tool from the older voice mail system, built for a different job.

questions: how is voicemail sent over email
what audio format does ivm use
is ivm the same as vpim
subtitle: How to send a voicemail as an ordinary Internet email that any mail client can still open and play.

tldr.problem: Unified messaging systems already sent voicemail over SMTP/MIME, but nothing standardized the details, and VPIM v2 messages were designed for voicemail-to-voicemail exchange and often cannot be used by an ordinary email client.
tldr.mechanism: IVM defines voice messages as normal Internet mail with a voice-message context, a multipart/mixed top level, critical-content marking and audio/basic (G.711 mu-law) audio that every recipient MUST be able to play.
tldr.outcome: Voicemail and email can share one infrastructure, and clients that do not know IVM can still play the audio. It is a Proposed Standard and is explicitly not a successor to VPIM v2.

today: RFC 4239 is a Proposed Standard from November 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself states that it is not a successor to VPIM v2 but an alternative for a different application.

sections.title: Why Voicemail Over Internet Mail
sections.content:
People sometimes prefer talking to typing, and carrying voicemail on top of Internet mail lets voice messaging and email stop living in separate worlds. The RFC also notes that devices without keyboards could take part in messaging this way.

Unified messaging systems could already send voicemail with SMTP/MIME, but without standardization they did not interoperate. VPIM v2 (RFC 2421, revised in RFC 3801) lets two voicemail systems exchange messages, but it was not designed for a desktop email client, and a VPIM v2 message is often not usable by an email recipient.

Internet Voice Messaging (IVM) is therefore a standard representation of a voicemail in SMTP/MIME plus a standard audio encoding that unified messaging systems and mail clients MUST implement. The abstract is explicit that IVM is not a successor to VPIM v2, but an alternative for a different application.
sections.eli5: Voice mail machines and email used to speak different languages. IVM lets a voice message ride in a normal email so your inbox can play it.

sections.title: The Voice Message Format
sections.content:
Every message MUST follow the Internet Mail format and MIME. A client that creates a voice message MUST set the message context to voice-message (RFC 3458), but recipients MUST NOT require it, so clients that do not know IVM still work. A receiver that sees the context SHOULD present the message as a voice message, not as an email with an attachment (RFC 4024).

The top-level content type of a new, forwarded or reply voice message SHOULD be multipart/mixed. multipart/voice-message MAY be used when the recipient is known to be VPIM v2 compliant.

If a message is useless without its audio, the audio part MUST be marked with a Criticality of CRITICAL on the Content-Disposition (RFC 3459). Non-essential parts, such as a vCard, MAY be marked IGNORE. When forwarding, clients MUST preserve the content type of all audio parts. A delivery notification MUST be a multipart/report, so that text-to-speech software can render it for the recipient.
sections.eli5: The envelope says 'this is a voice message', but the message still works even if the mail client cannot read that sticker. The important recording gets a 'must not lose' mark.

sections.title: Transport, Addressing and Notifications
sections.content:
Messages MUST travel by SMTP as updated by the DRUMS working group (RFC 2821). Delivery Status Notifications MAY be requested when delivery matters to the sender.

Any valid Internet mail address works for a voice message. The RFC points to related documents for onramp and offramp addressing (RFC 3804), mapping an E.164 phone number to a mailbox with ENUM (RFC 4238) and the VPIM LDAP schema (RFC 4237). When a message is stored from call answering, the caller's name and number MAY be kept in the headers.

Delivery Status Notifications MUST be supported, and any non-delivery MUST produce a notification if requested. If a receiving system supports content criticality but cannot process all the critical media types, it MUST refuse delivery of the entire message. Message Disposition Notifications SHOULD be supported, with the user deciding whether they are returned.
sections.eli5: The voice message goes through the normal postal system, and the post office will tell the sender if it could not be delivered.

sections.title: Voice Contents and Codecs
sections.content:
Voice content MUST be carried as audio/basic unless the sender knows the recipient can handle something else. Without knowledge of the recipient, a sender MUST use raw G.711 mu-law, which is audio/basic and SHOULD have a filename ending .au. audio/32kadpcm (G.726) MAY be used when the recipient is known to support VPIM v2.

Recipients MUST be able to play raw G.711 mu-law, and MAY play G.726 or other codecs. The VOICE parameter on Content-Disposition SHOULD mark spoken names and spoken subjects, and the Content-Duration header SHOULD give the audio length. Fax content SHOULD be carried per RFC 2532.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on one common kind of recording that every player understands. Fancier kinds are only for when you know the listener can play them.

sections.title: Interoperability with VPIM v2
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways IVM and VPIM v2 can work together. First, an IVM client that treats multipart/voice-message like multipart/mixed and can play audio/32kadpcm can at least use a VPIM v2 message. Care is needed so a reply does not become an invalid VPIM v2 message.

Second, a dual-mode system or client implements both specifications and picks one based on the message or the recipient's capabilities. How to find out what a recipient supports is outside the scope, and no standard solution had been defined.

Third, a gateway could translate between the two worlds by policy. For example, a VPIM v2 message with Sensitivity of Private might be rejected instead of being forwarded. A conformant IVM implementation MUST NOT send a non-VPIM v2 message to a system it knows to be VPIM v2, unless it knows the destination can handle it.
sections.eli5: There are two voice mail dialects. A client can understand both, or a translator in the middle can convert between them, but translating can lose details.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's main concern is the optional gateway between IVM and VPIM systems. Gateways are lossy, both when transcoding voice and when translating features, and different gateways could translate differently because the document does not define it. This may lead to unexpected behavior.

A gateway is also an extra point of attack. If compromised, it could carry out 'monkey in the middle' attacks that are hard to detect or look like authorized transformations. Aside from gateways, the RFC expects no new security issues beyond those in VPIM v2 and the other referenced RFCs, especially SMTP, the Internet Message Format and MIME.
sections.eli5: A translator in the middle might get the meaning slightly wrong, and a dishonest translator could change the message without anybody noticing.
